newsitem.title: USA: Emerging market bank supervision seen taking time.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market bank supervision seen taking time.

text.p: Leading bankers on Tuesday welcomed plans to improve bank supervision in emerging economies, but said it would be a long process and would not prevent all future banking crises.

The Institute of International Finance (IIF), which represents commercial banks and other financial institutions, said it would take time to implement all proposals from the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision.

"An effective, efficient banking supervision is not something which can happen overnight," IIF Deputy Managing Director John Haseltine told a news conference called to present a report from central European bankers.

He added: "Banking crisis in emerging markets over the last five or 10 years have been from combination of weak management and a weak supervisory system. You will never be able to eliminate problems in the banking industry."
IIF Managing Director Charles Dallara highlighted the need for adequate training and full debate between the supervisory authorities and the banks.
He said banks in central Europe had already made tremendous progress in improving management and risk management, but not all banks would stay in business.

"The weaker banks are not going to survive," he said. "Certainly there will remain problems, there will remain weak spots, but I think that a strong and transparent supervisory regime...combined with a competitive market place will go a long way to weeding out the week players."

The report from central Europe was the first response by banks in an emerging market region to the Basle Committee's proposals, and the IIF is also inviting bankers in other regions to give their views.
"The Central European working group concluded its report by stressing that financial market globalization is creating the need for greater harmonization of bank supervisory standards," the IIF said.
"This is happening at an opportune time for transition economies in Central Europe as they seek to create supervisory frameworks to support their market economies."
